title: Tech Talk: One bike to do it all? I think I’ve found the answer

Tech Talk: One bike to do it all? I think I’ve found the answer

Thanks to more than ten years testing products for Cyclist, tech editor Sam has plenty to say when it comes to new bikes and gear. Tech Talk is Sam’s fortnightly newsletter, with a focus that hops between his thoughts on the latest kit to be featured by Cyclist and wider tech trends that people are talking about, or should be talking about. Click here to get Tech Talk directly to your inbox.

In recent years a bit of a paradox has developed in the bike market where all bikes are getting more capable and yet the categories they sit in are getting more specific. Where originally there were just road bikes, there’s now things like endurance road, all-road (though the differences between those two are semantics more than anything else), lightweight race, aero race… and then there’s gravel.

Initially itself an offshoot of a road bike, even gravel has diverged into at least two categories, which potentially a third now splitting the difference as well (don’t believe me? Just ask Factor about its Sarana). Obviously cyclocross bikes continue to float somewhere in between everything, but given their specific design quirks, they’re excused from this particular discussion.

I can’t say I like this category expansion because it has more than a little to do with brands just trying to sell more bikes. It also makes it harder for new cyclists to access our hobby by increasing the likelihood of decision paralysis. However, it’s not all bad: the diversification of gravel has given rise to a type of bike that I think, for a lot of riders, can effectively consolidate several categories.

That kind of bike is the gravel race bike. Over the last year or so I’ve ridden four that stick out – Factor’s Aluto, Open’s Upper 2.0, BMC’s new Kaius and now Giant’s latest Revolt – for their ability to make any type of riding fun. Quick road rides? They give next to nothing away to road bikes. Easy gravel? They positively glide along. Gnarly single track? OK, it’s a bit white knuckle, but it’s never in doubt that they’ll get you down to the bottom of the trail in one piece.

Their versatility is explained in some of their stats. Take the Revolt for example – it weighs 6.95kg. That’s lighter than most road bikes and it’s got 45mm knobblies on. Weights like this combined with stiff, carbon spoked wheelsets means their acceleration is lively, but compliance is baked in via compact frameset geometry and skinny tube shapes, so they’re comfortable too.

Their fit geometry tends towards the aggressive, but not so much that it can’t be mitigated with a few spacers under the stem, and the handling geometry is pretty forgiving on different surfaces and tyre/wheels setups as well. Admittedly, it gets a bit goofy with narrow road tyres, but any slicks in the 34mm+ region will make the bike steer fine on the road. Off-road, these bikes now have the clearance to go up to mountain bike tyres. There’s no other category that allows this kind of build variety and works so well with it all.

With the increasing dominance of Sram’s excellent XPLR drivetrain, even their gearing gives the ride plenty of bandwidth. A 44t chainring still creates a sub-1:1 bottom gear with the 10-46 cassette and I challenge you to spin out on the flat in the 44-10. Campagnolo has a similarly versatile 1×13 drivetrain options and rumour has it, Shimano’s GRX will have an update next year as well, so gravel race bike gearing is just as flexible as the frameset designs.

Understandably, there will always be those that favour master-of-one type bikes (generally those that can afford more than one machine) and there’s still plenty to be said for that. But as my 500-odd words above show, there’s more than ever to justify the jack-of-all alternative thanks to the rise of the gravel race bike.

The rumour mill

Tech tip-offs from your man in the know

As I mentioned above, there has been whispers that the current GRX generation might be due for an update next year. For many, that’s likely to be welcome – the various guises of the current generation was rolled out in staggered fashion over a couple of years and the most important version of it – 1×12 wireless Di2 – is one sprocket behind SRAM and Campagnolo. 2027 might be the year we see Shimano’s gravel offering get back up to speed. If that’s the case it’ll be a big year for the brand, as we know Dura-Ace will show its new face in 2027 as well.

Tech tidbits

A couple of small product launch highlights from the last week or two

Silca tyres complete the ecosystem

Since Josh Poertner took over the historic Italian parts and accessories brand in 2013, Silca’s range has expanded steadily to include sealant, valves, TPU tubes, rim tape and a tyre pressure calculator alongside its famous pumps.

‘There was one product missing to complete the ecosystem,’ says Poertner. ‘The tyre itself. With that in mind, we’ve launched our Protocol series – three gravel models and one road option, the RCR.’

The RCR comes in 29, 34 and 38mm sizes. It might look like an eclectic mix, but the range was deliberate.

‘We engineered them specifically for modern rim profiles,’ he says. ‘29mm is the narrowest tyres that can officially fit on a 25mm internal rim width, for example. Unlike standard manufacturers who scale up narrow tyres as rims and clearances get wider, we started with the 38 mm model, which we believe to be the marquee tire in the road line up, and scaled down to 34mm and 29mm.

‘This means that rather than treating wide road tires as a traditional endurance options by adding layers of thick rubber (that compromises suppleness and speed) the 120 TPI Race Casing and low-rolling-resistance Pulsar compound in RCR tyres enable lower inflation pressures and wider contact patches in a fast, supple, lightweight package.’

Poertner claims practicality along with performance as well, explaining that the tyres use carbon fibre beads instead of Kevlar, ‘to guarantee dimensional stability and tool-free installation’, custom ply casing angles for suppleness and protection.

‘We even have thought to use a mould-release agent that plays nice with sealant – some can prevent proper adhesion and cause premature coagulation,’ says Poertner.

Mechanical shifting ain’t dead

Founded in the Lake District in 2018 by a pair Cambridge engineering graduates, Ratio Technology got its start making mechanical drivetrain upgrade kits – the small parts necessary to make 11-speed shifters and derailleurs compatible with newer 12-speed cassettes and chains, for example. The release of its own Mech was an extension of this business.

‘We already had three years of our shifting upgrade kit sales to prove to us that there was an appetite for reliable, serviceable mechanical shifting,’ says Ratio’s director, Tom Simpson. ‘Through these kits we built a “shopping list” of all the features we wanted to see on our own derailleur and built it to perform as well as an electronic one.’

Items on that list and present in the Mech include stainless bearings for all rotating components (rather than bushings) and a specific spring type and location inside the derailleur’s parallelogram to control the pull through the derailleur’s travel down the cassette.

‘The result is much less friction, so a light lever action without sacrificing return force. It makes the shifting much less sensitive to cable friction, contamination or imperfect cable routing,’ says Simpson.

Cannily, Ratio has made the Mech to be modular, so it isn’t locked into a specific manufacturer’s drivetrain.

‘By changing the cable fin or the cage length, the Mech can adapt to the bike or components around it,’ says Simpson. ‘We also design and manufacture it ourselves in the UK. That gives us particularly close control over the entire process, and means we can develop individual parts without having to redesign or replace the whole derailleur.’
